questions.stem: A 33-year-old man presented with a week of fever and tachypnea. He was known to have HIV infection but had disengaged with care. He did not take antiretroviral therapies nor any prophylaxis for opportunistic infections. He had no recent CD4 count or HIV viral load result. Investigations: Blood gas analysis revealed a PaO2 of 55 mmHg on room air (7.15 kPa) CXR: bilateral alveolar infiltrates BAL was positive for methenamine silver staining material
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate antimicrobial treatment?
questions.explanation: Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole (TMP–SMX) The patient in this clinical vignette presents with diffuse lung disease and is immunocompromised due to his HIV status. In addition, the patient has a silver stain that is positive, and he must be treated for pneumocystis pneumonia with TMP–SMX. The recommendation would also include administration of steroids due to the PaO2 being less than 60.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q13

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of dyspnea. His symptoms began as exertional dyspnea and dry cough but progressed to occurring at rest. He had ulcerative colitis and gout and was on treatment with infliximab. He had previously developed a Stevens–Johnson syndrome in response to sulfasalazine. He had also required blood transfusions after taking a new gout medication, which he could not remember. On examination, his respiratory rate was 32 breaths/ minute, and his oxygen saturation 85% on room air. Fine crepitations were heard throughout all lung fields. Investigations: Blood gas PaO2 55 mmHg (7.3kPa) Chest X-ray
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: Pentamidine This patient has severe pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). PCP is associated with a variety of immunocompromising conditions. It is a potential complication of most immunosuppressants, including TNF-α-antagonists like infliximab. He has a history of severe allergy to sulfasalazine, a sulfa agent, and thus TMP–SMX should be avoided. His history also hints at possible G6PD deficiency (he developed hemolytic anemia after taking rasburicase). His clinical findings of hypoxia and bilateral reticular opacification suggest the diagnosis. His disease is classified as severe based on PaO2 <70 mmHg. Atovaquone is not indicated for use in severe PCP . It can only be used in mild PCP . Clindamycin and primaquine are appropriate alternatives to TMP–SMX in severe PCP , but G6PD deficiency should be ruled out before use of primaquine given the patient’s history which raises concern for this disorder. TMP + dapsone are not indicated in severe PCP . Additionally, G6PD deficiency should be ruled out before use of dapsone given the patient’s history. (Image from Kumar P , Clark M. Kumar & Clark’s Cases in Clinical Medicine. 3rd ed. Elsevier; 2013.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q26

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presented with a worsening cough, shortness of breath, and fevers. He was known to have acute myeloid leukemia and had undergone a bone marrow transplant 3 months prior. He had occasionally required courses of corticosteroids to treat graft versus host disease. Investigations: CXR: bilateral interstitial infiltrates, worse in the lower lobes Bronchoscopy: bacterial and mycobacterial cultures negative An open lung biopsy was performed Lung tissue histology: numerous cells seen which are several times larger than surrounding cells with a central inclusion
questions.lead_in: What would be the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Ganciclovir The bone marrow transplant recipient is at risk for CMVassociated syndromes. Other risk factors for CMV disease in hematopoietic transplant recipients are the presence of graft versus host disease, CMV seropositivity, and older age. Cultures can be falsely negative, and results can take several days to return. Cytomegalic cells isolated from open lung biopsy are the pathologic hallmark of CMV infection, and they are characterized by a large size and the presence of intranuclear inclusions that are centrally placed. Ganciclovir would be the recommended therapy. CMV immune globulin has been used in combination with medical treatment for CMV pneumonitis but would not be recommended as the sole treatment. Letermovir is an antiviral drug that inhibits the CMV–terminase complex. It may have a role in the prophylaxis of CMV reactivation and disease in recipients of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplants but not in treatment of CMV disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q14

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. He denied a history of trauma, smoking, or chronic lung disease. He was known to have HIV with a history of nonadherence to his HIV medications and antibiotic prophylaxis. He also had a sulfa drug allergy. On physical exam, there were decreased breath sounds over the right upper lung fields with hyperresonance to percussion. Investigations: CXR: no pulmonary infiltrates seen; moderate-sized pneumothorax on the right lung CD4 count 122 cells/μL HIV viral load 2300 copies/mL Lactate dehydrogenase 560 U/L (122–222) 1,3-beta-D-glucan >500 pg/mL (<60) Qualitative serum cytomegalovirus (CMV) PCRpositive
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Clindamycin plus primaquine In a patient with HIV and CD4 <200 cells/ μL presenting with a spontaneous pneumothorax, a presumed diagnosis of Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) is strongly suspected. Given the sulfa drug allergy, clindamycin plus primaquine would be the appropriate treatment. The elevated LDH and 1,3-beta-D-glucan would also be consistent with PCP while this presentation would be less likely due to bacterial or endemic fungal pneumonias treated by the other answer choices. Although the CMV PCR was positive in the serum, CMV pneumonitis in HIV-infected patients (which would require ganciclovir) is very rare compared to PCP and usually requires lung biopsy for diagnosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q39

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with a 4-week history of worsening exertional dyspnea, dry cough, and mild fever. On examination his temperature is 37.9°C, his heart rate is 110 beats/minute, and his respiratory rate is 28 breaths/minute. Oxygen saturations are 90% on room air. He has oral candidiasis and small volume lymphadenopathy in his axillary, cervical, and inguinal chains. Auscultation of his chest is unremarkable. Investigations: Arterial blood gas PO2 (FiO2 room air) 7.8 kPa CXR: see radiograph below He is started empirically on intravenous trimethoprim– sulfamethoxazole (TMP–SMX) and methylprednisolone. On the second day of treatment he develops a widespread rash consistent with erythema multiforme, including oral ulceration and eye involvement. His TMP–SMX is identified as the likely cause.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment choice?

options.text: Continue TMP–SMX at a reduced dose of 90 mg/ kg per day
Start immediate desensitization regimen for TMP–SMX

questions.explanation: Switch to clindamycin plus primaquine This is the correct answer as the patient has presented with features of severe PCP and has developed a severe (grade 4) reaction to first-line treatment with TMP–SMX. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q35

needs: Chapter 310 — Infections in the Immunocompromised Host
questions.stem: A toddler presented with Pneumocystic jirovecii pneumonia, following a long-standing history of diarrhea, failure to thrive, and developmental delay. Laboratory examination revealed macrocytic anemia, leucopenia with hypersegmented neutrophils, and thrombocytopenia, as well as hypogammaglobulinemia.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hereditary folate malabsorption All these conditions can present with pneumocystis pneumonia. Cartilage–hair hypoplasia can also present with macrocytic anemia and short stature, but it lacks the other features of the disease (in particular, diarrhea and neurologic involvement). CD40L deficiency is accompanied by elevated IgM concentrations, while SP110 deficiency exhibits hepatic veno-occlusive disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q27

needs: Chapter 312 — Infections in HCT and Cellular Therapy Recipients
questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of shortness of breath and dry cough. There was no history of fever, hemoptysis, or coryzal symptoms. She had no sick contacts and no recent travel outside of the United States. She was 60 days postallogeneic stem cell transplant for acute myelogenous leukemia. She had previously had Stevens–Johnson syndrome due to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. She was taking levofloxacin, valaciclovir, voriconazole, and inhaled pentamidine. On examination, her temperature was 37.2°C, blood pressure was 132/65 mmHg, heart rate 105 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/minute, oxygen saturations 88% on 2LPM of O 2. Cardiovascular exam was unremarkable; respiratory exam revealed faint bilateral crackles. There was no pedal edema, and the rest of the exam was unremarkable. Investigations: Total white cell count 1.4 ×109/L Absolute neutrophil count 0.8 ×109 /L Hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL Platelets 98 ×109 /L eGFR >60 mL/min per 1.73 m2 LDH 340 U/L Blood cultures: no growth at 48 hours CXR: diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae, although can cause pneumonia in transplant recipients, would be unlikely given the levofloxacin prophylaxis, which is effective treatment for both of these pathogens. Typical findings on X-ray would be consolidations. Pulmonary aspergillosis would be unusual given the patient is on voriconazole prophylaxis, and typical findings on chest X-ray tend to be cavitations with aircrescent sign or nodules rather than interstitial infiltrates. MERS coronavirus can cause hypoxemia and interstitial infiltrates on chest radiography; however, the patient has not traveled to a part of the world affected by MERS coronavirus, such as the Middle East. Although the patient is receiving inhaled pentamidine for pneumocystis prophylaxis, this is not as effective as trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, and breakthrough infections have been reported. Thus the correct answer is Pneumocystis jirovecii.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q25

questions.question: A man on chronic prednisone admitted with fever and worsening cough and SOB. The respirologist decides to do a BAL for workup of possible PJP.

parts.text: Name 2 stains that can be used for PJP (specifically told not to use fluorescence or NAAT).

The BAL is positive for PJP. However, there was an induced sputum that was sent earlier which was reported as negative. What would lead you to believe that the first test was actually a false negative?

questions.model_answer: a) Two non-fluorescence, non-NAAT stains for PJP: (1) Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain. (2) Toluidine blue O (or Wright-Giemsa for trophic forms/cresyl violet as alternative). b) Reason first (induced sputum) test was likely false negative: BAL has substantially higher organism burden/sensitivity than induced sputum - induced sputum sensitivity is only ~50-60% versus BAL >90%, so a negative induced sputum does not reliably exclude PJP; also possible technical factors like inadequate specimen quality/volume on the sputum sample.

questions.model_answer: HIV-seronegative patients who should receive PJP prophylaxis (other than primary immunodeficiency), 4 groups: (1) Hematologic malignancy on intensive chemotherapy (e.g. ALL) or hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients. (2) Solid organ transplant recipients on immunosuppression. (3) Patients on prolonged high-dose corticosteroids (≥20 mg prednisone-equivalent daily for ≥4 weeks). (4) Patients on other significant immunosuppressive/biologic therapy for autoimmune disease (e.g. rituximab, cyclophosphamide, alemtuzumab) or with solid tumors on intensive chemotherapy.

questions.question: Glucocorticoids have been proven to have mortality benefits in certain infections. List 3 diseases, the associated pathogens and when glucocorticoids are indicated for each. Answer in this format for all 3.

parts.text: List 3 diseases, the associated pathogens, and when glucocorticoids are indicated for each (format: Disease / Pathogen / Steroid indication).

questions.model_answer:
Disease / Pathogen / Steroid indication:
(1) Bacterial meningitis / Haemophilus influenzae type b (children) / Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 2-4 days, given 20-30 minutes before or with the first dose of antibiotics (mortality/hearing-loss benefit demonstrated mainly in Hib meningitis).
(2) Bacterial meningitis / Streptococcus pneumoniae (adults) / Adjunctive dexamethasone given before or with the first antibiotic dose, shown to reduce mortality and unfavorable outcomes in adults with pneumococcal meningitis in resource-rich settings.
(3) Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia / Pneumocystis jirovecii (in HIV-infected patients) / Adjunctive corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone) indicated when room-air PaO2 <70 mm Hg or an alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient >35 mm Hg, started within 72 hours of anti-Pneumocystis therapy.

questions.question: You see a patient with a new diagnosis of HIV infection and pneumocystis pneumonia. They are requiring 4 L/min of supplemental oxygen to maintain their oxygen saturation >90%.

parts.text: The patient reports a history of full-body rash (but no mucous membrane involvement) to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 5 years ago. List FOUR alternate antibiotic or management options.
How soon should you start antiretroviral therapy?
List TWO criteria you should follow to discontinue prophylaxis for pneumocystis pneumonia.

questions.model_answer: a) Four alternatives to TMP-SMX (non-anaphylactic rash history, moderate-severe PJP requiring steroids given hypoxemia): (1) IV pentamidine. (2) Clindamycin plus primaquine (check G6PD first). (3) Consider TMP-SMX desensitization if clinically feasible given it remains most effective. (4) Atovaquone is an option but reserved for mild-moderate disease, not appropriate alone here given hypoxemia (4 L O2, moderate-severe disease); adjunctive corticosteroids required regardless of antibiotic choice given room air-equivalent hypoxemia (PaO2 <70 or A-a gradient >35). b) ART timing: start within 2 weeks of PJP diagnosis/treatment initiation (early ART improves survival, per ACTG 5164). c) Criteria to discontinue secondary PJP prophylaxis: CD4 count >200 cells/µL for at least 3 months on ART with sustained virologic suppression (undetectable viral load).

Ideal ART start: When stable and within 2 weeks of starting treatment for PJP. Stop prophylaxis criteria: CD4 counts increased from <200 cells/mm3 to >200 cells/mm3 for >3 months as a result of ART

questions.question: Name two second-line treatments for the following infections

parts.text: PJP pneumonia (other than TMP-SMX)
Toxoplasmosis (other than pyrimethamine)
Stenotrophomonas (other than TMP-SMX)

cohort_answer.text:
PJP pneumonia: Mild to moderate: Atovaquone; Clindamycin-Primaquine; Dapsone/TMP. Severe disease: Clindamycin-Primaquine (check for G6PD); IV Pentamidine (toxic). Prophylaxis: Dapsone; Atovoquone; Aerosolized pentamidine
Toxoplasmosis: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole monotherapy; Atovoquone alone; Atovoquone + sulfadiazine
Stenotrophomonas: Levofloxacin, moxi; Minocycline; Tigecycline; Ceftazidime (resistance is high); Colistin. Mechanism of resistance: multidrug-resistant efflux pumps, β-lactamases, and aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, reduced permeability of the outer membrane

questions.question: 18. Drug shortage in a hospital

parts.text: How would you treat the following conditions if the listed drug were not available? (3) Infection / Cannot Use / Treatment Options for: PJP, Toxoplasma, Stenotrophomonas

questions.model_answer: If preferred agent unavailable: PJP - TMP-SMX unavailable: use IV pentamidine (severe disease) or clindamycin plus primaquine (mild-moderate disease); atovaquone for mild disease/prophylaxis. Toxoplasma - preferred pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin unavailable: use TMP-SMX, or clindamycin plus pyrimethamine/leucovorin, or atovaquone-based regimen. Stenotrophomonas - TMP-SMX unavailable: use levofloxacin, or ceftazidime/minocycline, or combination of ticarcillin-clavulanate depending on susceptibility.

questions.question: 6 questions, fill in the blank with one of the options for 'I choose X over Y because'. Each answer can only be used once. Options: 1. Acyclovir over valacyclovir; 2. Valganciclovir over valacyclovir; 3. Famciclovir over acyclovir; 4. Atovaquone over dapsone; 5. Doxycycline over TMP-SMX; 6. Fluconazole over caspofungin; 7. Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate; 8. Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem; 9. Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin; 10. Metronidazole over clindamycin; 11. Azithromycin over clarithromycin; 12. Ampicillin over cloxacillin; 13. Cefazolin over cloxacillin

parts.text: I choose _______ because of better renal penetration
I choose _______ because I need a drug to cover for bacterial meningitis
I choose _______ because my patient has G6PD
I choose _______ because my patient is on carbamazepine
I choose _______ because it is not a drug that treats C. difficile and it is a drug that has not been strongly associated with causing C. difficile
I choose _______ because it has better activity for CMV

questions.model_answer:
a) Better renal penetration: Cefazolin over cloxacillin (cefazolin achieves high urinary concentrations; cloxacillin is highly protein-bound with poor urinary penetration).
b) Cover bacterial meningitis: Ampicillin over cloxacillin (ampicillin covers Listeria monocytogenes and achieves adequate CSF penetration; cloxacillin does not cover Listeria and penetrates the CNS poorly).
c) Patient has G6PD deficiency: Atovaquone over dapsone (dapsone causes oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency).
d) Patient on carbamazepine: Fluconazole over caspofungin (carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that reduces caspofungin exposure, requiring dose adjustment; fluconazole avoids this interaction).
e) Not a drug that treats C. difficile and not strongly associated with causing C. difficile: Doxycycline over TMP-SMX (doxycycline carries one of the lowest C. difficile risks among commonly used antibiotics and does not treat CDI).
f) Better activity for CMV: Valganciclovir over valacyclovir (valganciclovir is a ganciclovir prodrug with potent CMV activity; valacyclovir has only modest/prophylactic CMV activity and is primarily an HSV/VZV agent).

questions.question: Drug shortage in a hospital.

parts.text: How would you treat PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas infections if Septra, Sulfadiazine, and Ticarcillin/Clav or Septra respectively were not available? (give two treatment options each)
A patient with enterococcus infective endocarditis has high level aminoglycoside resistance. What is one issue with using streptomycin?

cohort_answer.text: PJP (no Septra): Severe: Pentamidine 4mg/kg IV, or Clindamycin 450mg PO q6h + Primaquine 15-30mg PO q24h x21d; Mild-moderate: Atovaquone 750mg PO BID with food x21d. Toxoplasma (no Sulfadiazine): Clindamycin 300mg PO q8h + Pyrimethamine, or Atovaquone 750mg PO BID + pyrimethamine. Stenotrophomonas (no Ticarcillin/Clav or Septra): Minocycline 200mg IV x1 then 100mg IV BID, or Levofloxacin 750mg IV/PO q24h, ceftazidime, colistin, cefiderocol. Streptomycin issue: high level resistance = growth in presence of high concentration of streptomycin or gentamicin, meaning no synergistic AG effect possible in vivo if resistant to both; cannot extrapolate resistance of one aminoglycoside based on the other
